Question: Does the platform maintain a centralised catalogue of approved models? Describe the registry.
Response: Yes. Three complementary layers. (1) Azure API Center is the unified registry: model metadata (provider, version, training provenance, licensing, regions, parameter counts), lifecycle stages (Design → Preview → Production → Deprecated), version history with author/timestamp/rationale, and cross-cloud reach (Azure-hosted Foundry models plus models from GCP/AWS/on-prem registered alongside). GitHub Actions sync from Git keeps the registry consistent with infrastructure-as-code. (2) Foundry Control Plane provides the platform model catalog itself (1900+ models) and surfaces evaluation/usage metrics. (3) APIM AI Gateway is the runtime governance layer: model routing policies define which models are accessible, with load balancing, failover, spillover, token limits, semantic caching, and cost tracking per model. Jurisdiction-based routing — EU-only model endpoints for GDPR-tagged workflows, US endpoints restricted per jurisdiction policy; residency metadata tracked per model deployment and enforced via APIOps CI gate. Models are selectable per skill — cheap models for triage tasks, frontier models for high-value reasoning — all governed centrally with one auditable record per call.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center (registry/lifecycle), Foundry model catalog, APIM AI Gateway (runtime governance), Foundry Control Plane

Question: Can you define and enforce metadata per model: training set provenance, data cutoff dates, licensing (FOSS vs proprietary), parameter counts?
Response: Foundry model catalog includes metadata per model: provider, version, licensing terms, parameter counts, capabilities, and supported regions. APIM AI Gateway policies can enforce constraints based on model metadata — e.g. restrict proprietary models to production environments only, or enforce region constraints (EU-only models for GDPR workflows). Model versioning in Foundry prevents silent updates: specific model versions are pinned in skill configurations and APIM routing policies. Training set provenance and data cutoff dates are available where model providers publish them, surfaced in the Foundry catalog.
Key Technologies: Foundry model catalog metadata, APIM policy enforcement

Question: Does the registry support model versioning to prevent silent updates from breaking agent behaviour?
Response: Yes. Model versions are pinned at two levels. (1) Skill-level: each SKILL.md can specify the model version it requires. (2) APIM-level: model routing policies reference specific model deployment versions. Model updates require explicit promotion through the CI/CD pipeline — a new model version is deployed as a separate endpoint, tested via Foundry Evaluators, and promoted only after passing quality gates. APIM supports blue-green model deployments: route a percentage of traffic to the new model version, compare quality metrics, and switch fully only after validation. Silent updates from model providers are prevented because we deploy specific model versions to Azure OpenAI endpoints, not floating latest versions.
Key Technologies: Foundry model deployments, APIM blue-green routing, skill model pinning

Question: Can administrators restrict model access by user group, agent sensitivity, or deployment environment? How do you prevent shadow AI (developers connecting to unapproved endpoints)?
Response: APIM AI Gateway is the single entry point for all model calls. No agent can bypass APIM to reach a model endpoint directly — network-level enforcement ensures all traffic routes through the gateway. Administrators restrict access by: (1) Agent identity — Entra RBAC scopes which models each Hosted Agent can access. (2) Environment — separate APIM configurations for dev/staging/production with different model allowlists. (3) Sensitivity — APIM policies can restrict frontier models to high-sensitivity workflows only. Shadow AI prevention: APIM is the only route to model endpoints

Question: Does the platform maintain a centralised catalogue of approved agents, including use-cases and risk levels?
Response: Yes. Two complementary registries. (1) Foundry Control Plane: provides a centralised agent inventory across all platforms (Foundry-native, custom, external) with lifecycle operations, risk classification, and compliance posture. (2) Azure API Center: registers skills with metadata — capabilities, allowed tools, risk level, lifecycle stage (Design/Preview/Production/Deprecated), version history. Since our architecture uses skills as the unit of specialisation inside a domain Hosted Agent — not N separate agent processes per role — the skill registry in API Center IS the functional agent registry. Each skill represents a specialised capability (screening, sourcing, compliance, offer generation) with its own metadata, tool allow-list, model assignment, and governance. This preserves WPP's heterogeneous team requirement while avoiding the overhead of 9+ separate agent identities, Conditional Access policies, and audit trails per domain. A2A is reserved for genuinely off-platform / cross-organisation agents (external partners, suppliers). See response §18 for the full Skills-vs-Multi-Agent trade-off analysis. Agent 365 adds another layer: agent registration in the M365 admin center with Entra Agent ID, Purview, and Defender integration.
Key Technologies: Foundry Control Plane, Azure API Center, Agent 365
POC Demo: POC1: Show skill registry in API Center with lifecycle states and risk levels.

Question: Can you define and enforce metadata per agent: capabilities, knowledge sources, tools employed, risk level?
Response: Yes. Each skill registered in Azure API Center carries enforced metadata: declared capabilities (what the skill does), allowed tools (which MCP servers it can invoke — enforced by GHCP SDK hooks), knowledge sources (which data stores it can access), risk level (determines HITL requirements and autonomy thresholds), lifecycle stage, and version. APIM policies enforce tool access per skill — a skill cannot invoke an MCP tool it has not declared. GHCP SDK session hooks enforce the tool allowlist at runtime: if a skill attempts to call an undeclared tool, the hook blocks it and logs the violation. Agent 365 extends this with Purview-enforced data classification and Defender threat detection per agent identity.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center skill metadata, GHCP SDK hooks (tool allowlisting), APIM policy enforcement, Agent 365

Question: Does the registry support agent versioning to support lifecycle management (dev to prod)?
Response: Yes. Azure API Center provides full lifecycle management for skills: Design -> Preview -> Production -> Deprecated. Each version is immutable once promoted. Version history is maintained with author, timestamp, and change description. Promotion between stages requires approval gates configured in the CI/CD pipeline. Skills are Git-synced — API Center integrates with GitHub Actions workflows for syncing SKILL.md files from repositories, so version control is native to the development workflow. Rollback is supported by promoting a previous version. Concurrent versions can run in different environments (v2 in staging, v1 in production) with environment-specific APIM routing.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center lifecycle management, Git sync, CI/CD approval gates

Question: Can administrators restrict agent access by user group, sensitivity, or deployment environment?
Response: Yes. Access restriction operates at multiple levels. (1) Entra RBAC: Hosted Agent containers have scoped Entra Agent IDs — the Hiring Agent and Finance Agent have separate identities with different tool access. (2) API Center lifecycle: skills in Design/Preview stages are not accessible in production environments. (3) APIM policies: per-environment, per-agent routing and access control. (4) Agent 365: administrators manage agent visibility and access in the M365 admin center — restrict which users can interact with which agents. (5) Control Plane UI: role-based views filter which workflows and capabilities are visible to each operator role. Conditional Access policies on agent identities enforce environment and compliance constraints.
Key Technologies: Entra Agent ID + RBAC, API Center lifecycle gates, APIM per-environment policies, Agent 365 admin

Question: Can the platform continually monitor third-party models for bias, drift, and robustness; generating alerts when test conditions fail?
Response: Yes. Foundry Evaluators run continuous evaluation on production traffic measuring: task adherence (is the agent doing what it should), tool call accuracy, safety, groundedness, and sensitive data exposure. Custom evaluators can be configured for bias detection and domain-specific quality metrics. APIM AI Gateway tracks per-model metrics: latency, error rates, token usage, cost — anomalies trigger alerts. The Fleet Manager agent consumes telemetry from Foundry Evaluators and APIM metrics, reasoning about fleet-wide quality trends. When evaluation scores drift below thresholds, the Fleet Manager surfaces alerts on the Control Plane with recommended actions (revert model version, adjust routing, increase HITL oversight). Azure Monitor and Application Insights provide the alerting infrastructure.
Key Technologies: Foundry Evaluators, APIM AI Gateway metrics, Fleet Manager agent, Azure Monitor
POC Demo: POC2: Show Foundry Evaluator running on CV screening output — detecting quality drift and alerting on Control Plane.

Question: How do you establish, authenticate, and manage the lifecycle of an agent's identity, including permissions, roles, and access controls?
Response: Entra Agent ID (part of Agent 365) establishes agents as first-class identities in Microsoft Entra ID. Each Hosted Agent container has a dedicated Entra Agent ID (e.g. hiring-agent@wpp, finance-agent@wpp, fleet-manager@wpp). The identity is domain-scoped: the Hiring Agent's identity grants access to Greenhouse, LinkedIn, Workday (hiring), Graph, and ACS — not finance systems. Lifecycle management: Agent 365 manages from creation to retirement with responsible person oversight throughout. Permissions: Azure RBAC scopes tool access per agent identity. OBO flows: when a human triggers an action, the GHCP SDK session (inside a MAF agent executor) can act on-behalf-of that human — audit trail attributes the decision to them, downstream access uses their delegated permissions. For autonomous phases, the session uses the Hosted Agent's app-only identity. Conditional Access policies apply to agent identities just as they do to human identities. Non-revocable actions (external email, offer letter, payment above threshold, ServiceNow JML, A2A outbound, Workday/D365 master data writes, compliance attestation, external publishing) are intercepted at GHCP SDK hooks inside the session and routed to the human's PA for approval — dual-control (two distinct Entra identities from two distinct operator groups) mandatory for high-risk. Tool calls carry JWT claims (skill ID, version, workflow phase, jurisdiction) validated at APIM against the per-skill tool allow-list — prompt-injected elevation attempts are rejected at the gateway.
Key Technologies: Entra Agent ID, Agent 365 lifecycle management, Azure RBAC, OBO flows, GHCP SDK hooks (non-revocable interception), APIM JWT claim validation, dual-control enforcement in DF
POC Demo: POC2: Show distinct agent identities in Entra with scoped permissions — Hiring Agent accessing only HR systems.

Question: How does the platform integrate with enterprise identity systems (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, Okta, Entra ID)?
Response: Full integration with WPP's identity landscape. Okta: primary IdP, federated via Entra External ID for SAML-bridged access to business systems (Workday, Greenhouse). Entra ID: native identity platform for all agent and human identities. OAuth 2.0 flows: Authorization Code (LinkedIn), Client Credentials (service-to-service), SAML-bridged (Workday via Okta), PKCE (web portal), Device Flow, OBO (Graph API calls on behalf of human). All auth complexity is abstracted at the platform level — agent developers do not manage tokens. APIM AI Gateway handles auth injection for all MCP tool calls. Automatic token refresh across all grant types without agent awareness. Azure Key Vault stores credentials with automated rotation.
Key Technologies: Entra ID, Entra External ID (Okta federation), APIM auth injection, Azure Key Vault

Question: How does the platform address auditability, non-repudiation, and secure credential management for agents?
Response: Auditability: every action is logged — OTEL spans capture tool calls with workflow context (who, what, when, why), APIM logs all model and tool interactions, Foundry Tracing provides full execution traces. All logs flow to Azure Log Analytics with 7-12 year retention (immutability enforced via Azure Storage export with immutability policies). Non-repudiation: Entra Agent ID ties every action to a specific agent identity. OBO flows attribute human-triggered actions to the human's identity. The action ledger in the workflow state store is append-only and maintains classification per action (revocable vs non-revocable from the Git-committed catalogue) with the identity/identities that authorised each — dual-control captures both operator identities for four-eyes approvals. Compensating transactions are recorded for reversals. Reasoning chain (OTEL traces from GHCP SDK and MAF) is stored separately from the action ledger in Log Analytics with correlated span IDs — auditors trace cause and effect without reasoning tokens becoming the audit record. Audit logs encrypted at rest with CMK via Key Vault; Azure Storage double encryption (service + infrastructure layer) on the immutable export. Secure credential management: Azure Key Vault stores all secrets (API keys, certificates, connection strings). APIM injects credentials into MCP tool calls at runtime — agent code never sees raw credentials. Automated credential rotation via Key Vault policies without agent downtime. Microsoft Sentinel provides security incident investigation across all audit data.
Key Technologies: OTEL tracing, Azure Log Analytics (immutable), Entra Agent ID, Azure Key Vault, Microsoft Sentinel
POC Demo: POC1: Show full audit trail for an invoice approval — trace from human decision through agent execution to system write-back.

Question: Describe supported tool-use patterns (MCP, REST/OpenAPI, etc.), tool registry, and tool-level access control.
Response: Tool-use patterns: (1) MCP — primary pattern. Enterprise systems exposed as MCP servers with typed tool definitions. GHCP SDK natively discovers and invokes MCP tools. (2) REST-to-MCP gateway — APIM auto-generates MCP tool definitions from OpenAPI specs, bridging REST APIs into the MCP ecosystem at build-time. (3) Logic Apps (low-code MCP) — visual workflows over 1,400+ prebuilt connectors exposed as MCP tools via APIM. (4) REST/OpenAPI — direct invocation via GHCP SDK tool definitions for systems that don't warrant a full MCP server. Tool registry: Azure API Center is the central, discoverable tool catalog with rich metadata (description, auth requirements, rate limits, SLA, owning team, supported environments, lifecycle stage), cross-cloud reach (tools hosted on Azure, GCP, AWS, on-prem registered in one registry), and Git-synced lifecycle management. APIM AI Gateway is the runtime governance layer (enforcement, auth injection, rate limits, content safety). Skills declare which tools they use. Agents discover available tools through API Center / APIM. Tool-level access control: per-skill tool allow-list compiled into APIM policy fragment at skill promotion via APIOps — enforcement sits in the gateway, outside the agent runtime, and cannot be bypassed by the LLM. Tool calls carry skill-context JWT claims (skill ID, version, workflow phase, jurisdiction) validated at APIM; a skill attempting to call an undeclared tool is rejected at the gateway before reaching the backend. GHCP SDK session hooks also enforce tool allowlists at runtime (defence-in-depth). Rate limiting per agent per tool. Content safety filtering on tool inputs/outputs.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center (tool registry, cross-cloud), MCP servers, Azure Logic Apps (low-code MCP), APIM REST-to-MCP gateway, APIM tool governance, GHCP SDK hooks
POC Demo: POC1: Show APIM tool catalog with registered MCP servers. Show hook blocking an undeclared tool call.

Question: Describe your platform's observability and management capabilities: traces, metrics, logs, dashboards.
Response: Four-layer observability spanning all three execution substrates. (1) Foundry Tracing (OTEL): MAF workflow graphs emit native execution spans (executor lifecycle, validator pass/fail, superstep boundaries); each GHCP SDK session inside a MAF agent executor emits spans via TracerProvider — model calls, tool calls, tokens, latency, cost. DF orchestration emits its own spans. Spans carry workflow ID, phase, MAF executor ID, jurisdiction, model, token count. Foundry Agent Monitoring Dashboard provides out-of-box visibility. (2) APIM AI Gateway metrics: token usage, latency, errors per model/tool/agent. Central cost tracking across all AI assets. (3) Fleet Manager assessment: event-driven reasoning over telemetry producing fleet health assessment, SLA risk analysis, anomaly detection, and exception prioritisation. This is the default Control Plane view — intelligent, not raw telemetry. Dashboards: Foundry Control Plane for platform-level monitoring. Custom Control Plane UI for operator experience (fleet dashboard, exception queue, situational awareness drill-down). Application Insights for deep technical investigation. Cost attribution per workflow, phase, model, and consumer visible across all dashboards.
Key Technologies: Foundry Tracing (OTEL), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 native spans, GHCP SDK OTEL TracerProvider, APIM metrics, Fleet Manager agent, Application Insights, Custom Control Plane UI
POC Demo: POC1: Show end-to-end OTEL trace for an invoice workflow — from intake through payment with cost attribution per phase.

Question: What mechanisms exist to intercept and intervene in an agent's execution loop in real-time?
Response: Four intervention mechanisms form a defence-in-depth stack. (1) GHCP SDK session hooks (`onPreToolUse`, `onPostToolUse`) intercept every tool call inside the agent executor session: non-revocable actions blocked, tool calls modified/redirected per runtime policy. (2) Foundry Guardrails intercept at four points (input, output, tool-call, tool-response) inside the agent executor — PII detection, task adherence, content safety. (3) MAF validator executors sit in the workflow graph between agent executors and downstream action executors — structural/policy enforcement on the typed output of the agent, the "judge catches executioner" pattern expressed as an explicit node and edge (not a prompt). If the validator rejects, the graph routes to a rejection or HITL branch. (4) APIM AI Gateway intercepts model and tool calls at the network layer — content filtering, token limits, rate limiting. For human intervention: operators can terminate workflows from the Control Plane (DF cancels, MAF checkpoints preserved); MAF supports native pause/resume within a phase for short-lived HITL; DF handles long HITL waits (days/weeks) across phases at zero compute. Agent-executor sessions are short-lived — the meaningful intervention points are the validator edge and the phase boundary. Fleet Manager surfaces workflows needing attention proactively.
Key Technologies: GHCP SDK hooks, Foundry Guardrails, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) validator executors + pause/resume, APIM AI Gateway, Control Plane UI, Azure Durable Functions suspend/resume
POC Demo: POC1: Demonstrate hook intercepting a payment execution, routing to Finance BP for approval, and deterministic execution after approval.

Question: Does the platform support enforcing policy-as-code to prevent excessive agency before an action completes?
Response: Yes. Policy enforcement operates through code-committed artefacts at every layer. (1) APIM policies version-controlled via APIOps CI/CD. (2) GHCP SDK hooks enforce rules inside the agent executor session (tool allowlisting, non-revocable interception, audit logging). (3) MAF workflow graphs and validator executors are Git-committed Python/.NET code: policy enforcement via validator nodes between agent executors is policy-as-code at the graph level. A new "judge" is a new validator executor with a PR. (4) Foundry Guardrails configuration per agent. (5) Autonomy thresholds in workflow configuration store, version-controlled, audit-trailed with operator identity for every change; safety-critical thresholds go through PR review rather than instant-apply sliders. (6) Jurisdiction-specific skills (SKILL.md per jurisdiction), loaded based on workflow context. (7) Non-revocable operations catalogue — Git-committed, PR-reviewed, audit-trailed: external email, offer letter, payment above threshold, ServiceNow JML ticket, A2A outbound, Workday/D365 master data writes, compliance attestation, external channel publishing. Revocability is a property of the tool, not of the skill. Dual-control / four-eyes is mandatory for high-risk actions (two distinct Entra identities from two distinct operator groups, enforced by Durable Functions). All policy artefacts Git-committed, PR-reviewable, audit-trailed.
Key Technologies: APIOps CI/CD, GHCP SDK hooks, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graphs + validator executors (policy-as-code), Foundry Guardrails, jurisdiction skills, Git version control
POC Demo: POC2: Show autonomy threshold change on Control Plane — audit trail captures who changed it, when, and why.

Question: Can we audit the specific model versions, system prompts, and tool definitions actively running in a given agent instance?
Response: Yes. Full inspectability at every level. (1) Model versions: OTEL spans record the exact model version used for every inference call (MAF workflow spans + GHCP SDK session spans). APIM logs model endpoint and version per request. (2) System prompts: skills (SKILL.md files) are the system prompts — Git-versioned, registered in API Center with version history. The exact skill version active in a workflow phase is recorded in the workflow state. (3) MAF workflow graph: the exact graph definition (executor types, edges, validator rules) active for a workflow is Git-versioned and recorded in the DF orchestration state; graph version is queryable per workflow. (4) Tool definitions: MCP tools available to each agent executor determined by the skill's declared allowlist, registered in APIM. OTEL spans record every tool call with parameters and results. All inspectable from Foundry Control Plane, Application Insights (KQL), Custom Control Plane UI.
Key Technologies: OTEL tracing (MAF + GHCP SDK), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graph versioning, Azure API Center version history, APIM logs, Application Insights KQL
POC Demo: POC1: Drill into a specific invoice workflow — show which skill version, model version, and tool definitions were active at each phase.

Question: How does the platform log and visualise the full chain-of-thought and execution path? Can we trace an action back to the reasoning step and tool call that triggered it?
Response: Full traceability through OTEL instrumentation across all three execution layers. Durable Functions emits orchestration spans. MAF workflow graph execution emits native spans per executor (lifecycle, validator pass/fail, superstep boundaries). Each agent executor invokes a GHCP SDK session that emits spans capturing skill loaded, model + version, reasoning, tool calls (parameters and results), decisions. Spans are correlated by workflow ID, phase and MAF executor ID, creating a complete execution graph. Visualisation: Foundry Tracing for raw traces with reasoning steps and validator outcomes. Application Insights supports KQL queries for cross-workflow analysis. Custom Control Plane UI provides click-through situational awareness. Trace-to-action: every entry in the action ledger links back to the OTEL span that produced it, including reasoning chain, validator verdict and tool call.
Key Technologies: Foundry Tracing (OTEL spans), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 native spans, GHCP SDK OTEL TracerProvider, Application Insights, Custom Control Plane UI, action ledger
